_changelog: v1.0.0 (2026-10-07) first version. Board cards use the catalog's four a1e08 concept ids (scaling-laws, model-sizes, frontier-vs-small-open-models, choosing-a-model); strings reach back to weights (a1e02), tokens (a1e03), context-windows (a1e05), pretraining (a1e07) and overfitting (a1e01, whose rule of thumb this case bends as promised) and ahead to why-evals and golden-sets (a5e01), routing-to-cheaper-models (a6e04) and statelessness (a1e09). Honours the a1e07 tease: a library that keeps growing, a reader that gets cleverer with every new wing, and the night a small one answered better than the big one
title: Bigger Isn't Always Better

post.author: u/night_stacks_eskil
post.title: My library builds a bigger reader for every new wing, and each one has been cleverer than the last. Last night the small one in the old reading room answered a question the newest one couldn't.

blocks.text: I'm a junior developer and the night systems person at the Wexcombe Library, which has added a wing a year since 2024. Every wing gets a reader: a language model we train from scratch on the library's own text, then teach to answer questions at that wing's night desk. The chair of the trustees, Mr Lysander Crabbe, has one rule for readers: more shelves, more mind. By shelves he means parameters, and each new reader gets twice as many as the last: 1 billion for the West Wing, 2 for the East, 4 for the New Wing this spring.

The training compute is an allowance from a university consortium, counted in operations, and it has doubled every year. The books haven't. Every wing's reader has read the same thing: the catalogue, every book we own, typed up, 20 billion tokens. Each one still finished training with a lower loss than the one before, and Mr Crabbe frames every log.

This spring the consortium gave the old reading room an allowance too, the same size as the New Wing's, and Ottoline Pyke, our archivist, built it a reader in her last month before she retired. The trustees told her it could be small.
At 2:14 last night a woman at the New Wing desk asked for a book her grandmother read as a girl: a green cover, a hot-air balloon, a cat called Admiral.

02:14  new wing desk      Over the Rooftops, by Tamsin Corliss, 1931. Shelf N4-112.
02:17  shelf N4-112       empty. no such title anywhere in the catalogue.
02:21  reading room desk  The Admiral Goes Up, by Elspeth Varley, 1934. Shelf R1-07.
02:24  shelf R1-07        green cover. a balloon. a cat called Admiral.
The smallest reader in the building is the cleverest one.

So I ran the enquiry book on the three readers still at a desk: 400 questions patrons have asked over the years, with the answers our reference librarians gave. The reading room's reader got 352 right. The New Wing's got 324, the East Wing's 300. The West Wing's was switched off last year. Then I copied out the training logs.

The trustees vote on Friday. They want the New Wing reader on every desk, and next year's allowance, twice this one, spent on an 8-billion-parameter reader for the North Wing, trained on the catalogue as always. What do I tell them?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in that library is haunted. Some names for what's on your logs. A model's size is its number of parameters, the dials from case 2, written like 4B for 4 billion. Training compute is counted in FLOPs, floating-point operations, and a common approximation is 6 × parameters × tokens read; the FLOPs you can spend on one training run are its compute budget, your allowance. A scaling law is a formula, fitted to many training runs, that predicts a model's loss from its size and the tokens it reads. Two questions. The New Wing reader and Ottoline's had the same budget: what did each one spend it on? And at your desks, what does each reader cost you on every question, in money and in waiting?

replies.author: u/night_stacks_eskil
replies.text: Same budget to the last operation: 6 × 4B × 20B and 6 × 1B × 80B both come to 4.8 × 10^20. The New Wing's went on shelves: 5 tokens read for every parameter. Ottoline's went on reading: 80 for every parameter. And per question, the contractor prices our readers at $0.10 per million tokens for every billion parameters, so the New Wing's costs four times the reading room's. It takes 1.4 seconds to answer, the East Wing's 0.8, the reading room's 0.5.

comments.author: u/deposit_boxes_ottoline
comments.text: This is Ottoline. The trustees gave me the allowance and never asked what I meant to do with it, so I'll tell you. For eleven winters, volunteers typed up the basement: every newspaper, pamphlet and letter the library has been sent since 1826, sixty billion tokens of it. My reader read all of that and the catalogue, once each. It has read more than anyone in that building.

replies.author: u/night_stacks_eskil
replies.text: Thank you. I went down to the basement tonight. Every box has a card on its lid in your handwriting, and every card says the same word: read.

comments.author: u/ticket_sorter_odalys
comments.text: I look after the model that sorts an online shop's support tickets into six queues. Last spring we moved it off a small open-weight model, one whose parameters you can download and run on your own machines, onto a frontier model, the biggest and most capable kind the big providers sell, because it topped a benchmark: a public set of test questions that every new model gets scored on. Our bill went up thirty times, and the latency, the wait for each answer, went from half a second to three. My manager still opens every meeting with the benchmark chart.

replies.author: u/night_stacks_eskil
replies.text: I tried one this evening. I sent the enquiry book to a hosted frontier model, names stripped, since our rules say a patron's question only leaves the building without the name: 380 of 400, at $8 per million tokens, 2.6 seconds an answer. The desks get about 10,000 questions a night, mostly through the website, about 2,000 tokens each with the answer. And Mrs Quarmby, the head librarian, won't put anything on a desk that gets fewer than 340 right.

reply.prompt: The trustees vote on Friday: the New Wing reader on every desk, and next year's doubled allowance on an 8B reader for the North Wing. What should Eskil tell them? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Put the smallest reader that clears Mrs Quarmby's 340 on every desk, send what it's unsure of up to a bigger model, and spend next year's allowance on a reader sized to read everything we own.
options.part2: I took the enquiry book and the logs to the meeting. The reading room reader is the smallest that clears 340: 352 of 400, $60 a month on the desks against the New Wing reader's $240, and 0.5 seconds an answer. It went on every desk on Monday. The questions it marks unsure, about one in ten, have the names stripped and go to the hosted model, and the whole bill is $534 a month. Then the North Wing. On the catalogue alone, the 8B plan predicts a loss of 2.401, a hair under Ottoline's 2.408 for twice the compute, at eight times her reader's cost on every question. The same allowance on a 2B reader that reads all 80 billion tokens predicts 2.333, within a thousandth of the best split the formula allows. Mr Crabbe asked how many shelves that was. Half the New Wing's. He voted for it anyway. At 2:14 tonight a man asked the New Wing desk for the cat in the balloon. It sent him to R1-07.
options.senior: Choose a model with your own test: the smallest that passes, with the hard cases sent up, because size costs you on every call. And a fixed training budget buys parameters and tokens together; a bigger model that reads too little is an expensive way to be worse.

options.text: Agree to both. One strange night and 400 old questions can't outweigh three years of logs in which every wing's reader beat the last, so an 8B North Wing reader will be the cleverest one yet.
options.part2: The trustees voted for both. The New Wing reader went on every desk on Monday: 324 of 400 on the enquiry book, under Mrs Quarmby's bar, at $240 a month against the reading room's $60, and 1.4 seconds an answer. By Thursday it had sent patrons to eleven empty shelves. And the logs had promised less than the trustees heard. The 8B North Wing reader, on the same catalogue, predicts 2.401: a hair under Ottoline's 2.408, for twice her compute, and eight times her reader's cost on every question it will ever answer.
options.senior: A scaling law says loss falls as size grows with the data fixed, but by less each time, and the data sets a floor: on 20 billion tokens, no number of shelves takes this formula below 2.226. A smooth trend in your logs isn't a test of your task.

options.text: Put the hosted frontier model on every desk instead. It got 380 of 400, the best of any reader, and the library can hand next year's allowance back to the consortium unspent.
options.verdict: Trade-off: the best answers, the biggest bill
options.part2: We put the hosted frontier model on every desk for a week, names stripped as our rules require. It was the best reader the library has had: 380 of 400 on the enquiry book. It was also $4,800 a month against the reading room reader's $60, and 2.6 seconds an answer against 0.5. On Wednesday a man asked it to find his late wife's letters in the basement, and wrote her full name and their address into the question. Stripping his name hadn't stripped hers, and it left the building. The trustees kept the hosted model for the website's hardest questions only, and gave the allowance back. Nobody is building the North Wing reader.
options.senior: A frontier model is often the most capable, and you pay for that on every call: in money, in waiting, and in where your users' words go. Send it the questions a smaller model can't answer, not all of them.

options.text: Let a famous public benchmark settle it. Thousands of exam questions say far more than 400 old enquiries do, so whichever reader scores highest on the benchmark goes on every desk.
options.part2: I scored the three readers on a famous public benchmark: thousands of school exam questions, four choices each. Reading room 27 percent, East Wing 26, New Wing 29. A reader guessing at random would get 25. The trustees saw the New Wing on top and voted it onto every desk, and the 8B reader into next year. Not one of the exam questions asked where a book is shelved. The desks now send someone to an empty shelf about once a night.
options.senior: A public benchmark measures its own questions, not your task, and close to the score of random guessing its differences are noise. Choose with a test built from your users' real questions, judged the way they will judge the answers.

sim.title: Split the allowance, then choose a reader
sim.lede: You're Eskil at ten past three with the training logs open. Part A predicts loss with the formula DeepMind researchers fitted in 2022 to over 400 training runs: L = E + A/N^α + B/D^β, where N is parameters, D is tokens read, and the constants are as printed in their paper: E = 1.69, A = 406.4, B = 410.7, α = 0.34 and β = 0.28. Treating the library's text as if it behaved like theirs is a teaching simplification. Pick a compute budget in FLOPs. The paper's approximation, compute = 6 × N × D, about six operations for every parameter for every token read, then fixes how many tokens each size can afford. The curve is the predicted loss of every split of that budget; the parameters axis is a log scale, where each step multiplies by ten. The best-split dot sits at the bottom of the curve, the larger dot is the size you chose, the labelled dots are the library's readers at their own budgets, and the small dots are the best loss at every budget in the list. Part B lines up the four readers Eskil could put on the desks, with the enquiry-book scores and answer times from his replies and the contractor's prices, which are teaching prices like case 3's. It picks the smallest that clears Mrs Quarmby's bar and prices a month of 30 nights at 10,000 questions a night.
sim.tryThis: Try this: you start on the New Wing reader, 4.8 × 10^20 FLOPs on 4B parameters. It can read 20.0 billion tokens, and the predicted loss is 2.447. The best split for that budget is 1.31B parameters on 61.1 billion tokens, 2.405. Slide the parameters down to 1B: 80.0 billion tokens and 2.408, Ottoline's reader, a whisker from the best. Slide them up to 8B: only 10.0 billion tokens fit, and the loss rises to 2.515. Set the compute to 1.2 × 10^20 and the parameters to 1B for the West Wing's 2.580, then 2.4 × 10^20 and 2B for the East Wing's 2.506: each doubling helped, by less each time. Set 9.6 × 10^20, next year's allowance: 8B reads the catalogue for 2.401, and 2B reads all 80 billion for 2.333, against a best split of 1.79B at 2.333. Then 5.76 × 10^23, the budget DeepMind spent on its 280B model, Gopher: 70B gives 1.938 and 280B gives 1.984, and the formula's own best is 32.2B. In Part B the bar starts at 85 percent, 340 of 400, and the reading room reader clears it for $60.00 a month. Raise the bar to 89 and only the frontier model clears it, at $4,800.00. Put it back to 85 and send 10 percent of questions up: $534.00.

explain.oneLine: Nothing at the Wexcombe Library is haunted. Every training run spends its compute on two things, parameters and tokens read. The trustees kept buying shelves for the same 20 billion tokens of books; Ottoline spent the New Wing's compute on a reader a quarter its size that read four times as much, and it came out cleverer, cheaper and faster.

steps.title: A training run spends its compute on two things: parameters and tokens.
steps.text: A model's size is its number of parameters, the dials from case 2. Its data is counted in tokens read, the pieces of text from case 3. Training works every parameter for every token, so the compute grows with both, and the Chinchilla paper uses the approximation FLOPs ≈ 6 × N × D, where N is parameters and D is tokens. That's why the New Wing reader, 4B on 20 billion tokens, and Ottoline's, 1B on 80 billion, cost exactly the same: 4.8 × 10^20 FLOPs each. The paper notes that the compute budget is often known in advance, so the real question is how to split it. For a fixed budget, every extra shelf means fewer books read.

steps.title: Scaling laws: loss falls smoothly, by less each time.
steps.text: In 2020 Kaplan and colleagues at OpenAI found that a language model's loss scales as a power-law with model size, dataset size, and the amount of compute used for training: smooth enough that small runs predict big ones. The Chinchilla paper, from DeepMind in 2022, fitted one formula to the final losses of its runs: L(N, D) = E + A/N^α + B/D^β, with E = 1.69, A = 406.4, B = 410.7, α = 0.34 and β = 0.28 (Appendix D.2, equation 10). E is the loss even a perfect model would have, the paper's entropy of natural text; the second term shrinks as the model grows, the third as it reads more. Each doubling of parameters cuts the second term by the same share, to 0.79 of what it was, so it buys less each time: the West, East and New Wing readers came out at 2.580, 2.506 and 2.447, drops of 0.074 and then 0.059. With the books fixed, the third term never moves: on 20 billion tokens, no number of shelves takes this formula below 2.226. The readers really did get cleverer with every wing, toward a floor set by the books.

steps.title: Compute-optimal: at a fixed budget, a smaller model that reads more can win.
steps.text: For a fixed budget the formula draws a valley. Too few parameters and the model can't hold what it reads; too many and it can't afford to read enough. At 4.8 × 10^20 the bottom of the valley, from the paper's equation 4, is about 1.31B parameters on 61.1 billion tokens, loss 2.405. Ottoline's reader, at 2.408, sits almost on it. The New Wing reader, at 2.447, is well up the other side, and an 8B reader on the same allowance could read only 10 billion tokens, for 2.515. The paper's headline is the same trade at full size. Gopher, DeepMind's 280 billion parameter model, was trained on 300 billion tokens. Chinchilla used the same compute budget with 70 billion parameters and 1.4 trillion tokens, and it outperformed Gopher across the large range of tasks the paper tested. From over 400 training runs the authors concluded that for compute-optimal training, the model size and the number of training tokens should be scaled equally: for every doubling of model size the number of training tokens should also be doubled. Kaplan's analysis had said that for 10 times the compute, size should grow 5.5 times and tokens only 1.8 times. Most large models of the day had been trained on about 300 billion tokens, and the paper called them significantly undertrained.

steps.title: Case 1's rule bends for big networks, and held-back error stays the judge.
steps.text: Case 1 said a model wants many more examples than numbers to tune, and promised the rule would bend here. In a language model every next token is an example, and Gopher read about one token for every parameter: 300 billion for 280 billion. Case 1 would have worried about memorizing. But big language models usually read their text only once, and the Chinchilla paper's runs read fewer tokens than their corpus holds, so the authors treat training loss as an unbiased estimate of the test loss. For big networks trained this way, the failure the paper found is not memorizing but reading too little for the compute spent: undertrained. Chinchilla was trained at about 20 tokens per parameter, and Ottoline's reader at 80. Meta's Llama 3 8B kept improving on up to 15 trillion tokens, far past the about 200 billion that Meta calls Chinchilla-optimal for its size, because, in Meta's words, smaller models are generally preferred because they are much more efficient during inference. The judge hasn't changed: loss on text the model never trained on, and your own test.

steps.title: Choosing a model for a product: your own test, then the smallest that passes.
steps.text: Most engineers don't train models; they choose one, and the same lesson holds: size is a cost, not a guarantee. A frontier model is usually the most capable on hard, open-ended work. A small or open-weight model is cheaper and faster on every call, and an open-weight one can run on your own machines, which matters when, as at the library, questions may not leave the building as asked. Compare candidates on what the product needs: quality on your own task, measured on real questions with known answers rather than assumed from size or a public benchmark; price per million tokens times your volume; latency; whether your longest input fits the context window from case 5; and where the data goes. Then put the smallest model that passes your bar into service, and send the cases it is unsure of to a bigger one. Anthropic's guide to choosing a model offers two starting points, efficiency-first and capability-first, and in both the deciding step is the same: create benchmark tests specific to your use case. At the library's desks, the reading room reader clears 340 of 400 with 352 for $60 a month; sending one question in ten up to the hosted model makes the bill $534. Season 5 builds those tests, and Season 6 the routing.

diagram.aria: Training and choosing, with Eskil's numbers. Top half: a compute budget, about 6 times N times D FLOPs, here 4.8 times 10 to the 20, is spent on parameters, N, the shelves, 1B or 4B, and on tokens read, D, the books, 80B or 20B. Both feed the predicted loss, E plus A over N to the alpha plus B over D to the beta, 2.408 or 2.447. A note says loss guides training and your own test picks the model. Bottom row: your own test, 400 enquiries, bar 340 right, leads to the smallest reader that passes, the reading room's with 352, 60 dollars a month, which sends questions it is unsure of up to a frontier model, 534 dollars a month in all.

notes.text: loss guides training; your own test picks the model

explain.caption: Top: a compute budget, about 6 × N × D FLOPs, is spent on parameters and tokens together, and the formula predicts the loss from both: Ottoline's 1B on 80 billion tokens comes out at 2.408, the New Wing's 4B on 20 billion at 2.447, on the same budget. Bottom: loss guides training, but a product is chosen by its own test. The smallest reader that clears the bar goes on the desks, and the questions it is unsure of go up to a bigger model.

fix.title: The fix: spend compute on reading as well as shelves, and choose by your own test
fix.text: When you train, fix the budget first, then choose the split. A scaling law fitted to small runs shows where the valley is for your compute, and before you buy size, check that you have enough fresh text for it to read. When you choose a model, write the test first: a few hundred real questions with known answers, and a bar agreed before anyone looks at a score. Run every candidate on it, from the smallest up, and include one frontier model to see what the ceiling looks like. Price each one at your real volume, measure its latency, and check where it sends your data. Put the smallest that passes into service, send what it is unsure of to a bigger model, and run the test again whenever a model, a prompt or your users' questions change.

limits: The formula is a fit to one lab's runs on one dataset, and this case uses its rounded, printed constants. With them, the best split at Gopher's budget is about 32 billion parameters at about 93 tokens each, while the paper's own Figure 4 projects 40 billion and its other two methods 63 and 67 billion. Epoch AI's 2024 replication traced the gap to rounding and to a fit that stopped too early, and its refit implies about 20 tokens per parameter; with its constants, every comparison in this case still comes out the same way. Use a scaling law for direction, and fit your own when the money matters.

Compute-optimal means the lowest loss for the training compute, not the cheapest model to run. A model that will answer millions of questions can be worth training smaller and longer than the best split, as Meta did with Llama 3, and as Ottoline's reader, at 80 tokens per parameter, already is. The formula was also fitted on runs that never repeated their text, so it says nothing about reading the same books twice.

Your own test only covers its questions. 400 enquiries can miss whole kinds of question, a bar of 340 is a judgment, and a bigger model costs more on every call for as long as it runs, so test again when the questions change. And no size of model remembers yesterday's desk: each question starts from nothing, which is case 9.

explain.seniorTake: Size is a cost, not a guarantee. A fixed training budget buys parameters and tokens together, and a bigger model that reads too little is an expensive way to be worse. For a product, choose with your own test: the smallest model that passes, the hard cases sent up, and the test run again whenever anything changes.

realWorld.title: Chinchilla, 2022
realWorld.text: Jordan Hoffmann and colleagues at DeepMind trained over 400 language models ranging from 70 million to over 16 billion parameters on 5 to 500 billion tokens, and asked how a fixed compute budget should be split. Their answer: for compute-optimal training, the model size and the number of training tokens should be scaled equally: for every doubling of model size the number of training tokens should also be doubled. They tested it on Gopher's budget. Gopher had 280 billion parameters and 300 billion tokens; Chinchilla had 70 billion parameters and 1.4 trillion tokens, and both Chinchilla and Gopher have been trained for the same number of FLOPs. Chinchilla outperformed Gopher across the paper's large range of tasks, and the paper notes that, being 4 times smaller, both the memory footprint and inference cost of Chinchilla are also smaller. The abstract's verdict on the field: current large language models are significantly undertrained, a consequence of the recent focus on scaling language models whilst keeping the amount of training data constant.

realWorld.title: Scaling laws, 2020
realWorld.text: Jared Kaplan and colleagues at OpenAI studied empirical scaling laws for language model performance on the cross-entropy loss. The loss scales as a power-law with model size, dataset size, and the amount of compute used for training, with some trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude, while other architectural details such as network width or depth have minimal effects within a wide range. Their advice on spending compute is the one Chinchilla revised: larger models are significantly more sample-efficient, such that optimally compute-efficient training involves training very large models on a relatively modest amount of data and stopping significantly before convergence. The Chinchilla paper traces part of the difference to method: Kaplan's runs used a fixed number of training tokens and learning rate schedule for all models.

realWorld.title: The formula, and its printed constants
realWorld.text: The Chinchilla paper's third method fits L(N, D) = E + A/N^α + B/D^β to the final losses of its runs (equation 2, section 3.3) and reports E = 1.69, A = 406.4, B = 410.7, α = 0.34 and β = 0.28 (equation 10, Appendix D.2). The first term, it says, should correspond to the entropy of natural text; the second captures the fact that a perfectly trained transformer with N parameters underperforms the ideal generative process; the final term captures the fact that the transformer is not trained to convergence. Minimizing it under the constraint FLOPs(N, D) ≈ 6ND gives the best split in closed form (equation 4), which this case's sim uses directly. The paper notes that the third approach predicts even smaller models being optimal at larger compute budgets, and its Figure 4 projects 40 billion parameters for Gopher's budget, 5.76 × 10^23 FLOPs.

realWorld.title: A replication, 2024
realWorld.text: Tamay Besiroglu, Ege Erdil, Matthew Barnett and Josh You at Epoch AI rebuilt the data from the Chinchilla paper's plots and refit the formula. They found the reported estimates inconsistent with the paper's first two methods and traced it to two causes: the optimizer used by Hoffmann et al. stopped before convergence, and the parameter estimates reported in the body of the paper are rounded in a way that results in substantial bias in the predictions. The scaling policy from Hoffmann et al.'s estimates suggests about 70 tokens per parameter, out of step with the roughly 20 that Chinchilla itself was trained on. Their refit, E = 1.8172, A = 482.01, B = 2085.43, α = 0.3478 and β = 0.3658, implies about 20 tokens per parameter, consistent with the paper's first two methods and with how Chinchilla was trained.

realWorld.title: Llama 3, 2024
realWorld.text: Meta's April 2024 post on Llama 3 shows both uses of a scaling law. Scaling laws, it says, allow us to predict the performance of our largest models on key tasks before we actually train the models. And while the Chinchilla-optimal amount of training compute for an 8B parameter model corresponds to ~200B tokens, we found that model performance continues to improve even after the model is trained on two orders of magnitude more data. Both its 8B and 70B models continued to improve log-linearly after training on up to 15 trillion tokens. Its reason for training small models so long is the cost of running them: larger models can match the performance of these smaller models with less training compute, but smaller models are generally preferred because they are much more efficient during inference.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: choosing a model
realWorld.text: Anthropic's guide to choosing a model, as checked in October 2026, says that choosing means balancing capabilities, speed, and cost, and offers two ways to start. Efficiency-first: begin with a faster, more cost-effective model, test your use case thoroughly, evaluate if performance meets your requirements, and upgrade only if necessary for specific capability gaps; it lists this as best for applications with tight latency requirements, cost-sensitive implementations and high-volume, straightforward tasks. Capability-first: implement with the strongest starting point for your task, then optimize to more efficient models down the line, for complex tasks where intelligence and advanced capabilities are paramount. Either way, to decide whether to change models, create benchmark tests specific to your use case, since having a good evaluation set is the most important step in the process, and test with your actual prompts and data. The guide also describes pairing models: multi-model strategies pair a lower-cost model with a frontier model so that most tokens are billed at the lower rate, for example an executor that escalates hard decisions to an advisor.

asked: How do you choose a model for a use case?
What do scaling laws say, and what did Chinchilla change?
When is a small model the right call?
interview.answer: I choose with my own test, not by size or a public benchmark. First I write down what the feature needs: the quality bar on our real inputs, the latency users will tolerate, the volume, the longest input it has to fit in the context window, and where the data is allowed to go. Then I build a test set of real examples with known answers and agree the bar before scoring anything. I run candidates from small open-weight models up to a frontier model, which also shows me the ceiling, price each one at our real volume, and measure latency. I ship the smallest that passes, send the cases it's unsure of to a bigger model, and re-run the test whenever a model, a prompt or the traffic changes. Scaling laws say a model's loss falls smoothly and predictably as parameters, training tokens and compute grow, as power laws with diminishing returns, so small runs can predict big ones. Kaplan and colleagues in 2020 read that as: spend extra compute mostly on bigger models. Chinchilla in 2022 found that for a fixed compute budget, model size and training tokens should be scaled equally, doubling the tokens with every doubling of parameters, and that many large models were undertrained: its 70B model on 1.4 trillion tokens beat the 280B Gopher, trained on 300 billion with the same compute. A small model is the right call when it passes your own test at your bar: high-volume, straightforward tasks like classification or extraction, tight latency, tight budgets, or data that has to stay on your own machines. Its savings in cost and time apply to every call for as long as it runs, which is also why labs now train small models on far more tokens than compute-optimal, as Meta did with Llama 3.

terms.def: This case's word for the library's language models: each trained from scratch on the library's own text, then taught to answer questions at a night desk.
The library's word for its compute budget: the training compute a university consortium lends it each year, doubled every year so far.
A group of organisations that share something. Here, universities that share their computers.
Eskil's test set: 400 questions patrons have asked over the years, with the answers the reference librarians gave. Season 5 calls a set like this a golden set.
How big a model is, counted in parameters, the dials from case 2. Written like 4B for 4 billion. Bigger models cost more to train and more to run.
Short for billion when counting tokens too: 20B tokens is 20 billion. Case 7 used it for parameters.
The total arithmetic a training run does, counted in FLOPs. It grows with both the model's size and the number of tokens it reads.
A floating-point operation: one arithmetic step, like a multiplication, on numbers with a decimal point. Training compute is counted in FLOPs: 4.8 × 10^20 for the New Wing reader.
The FLOPs you can afford for one training run, often fixed before training starts. The library's allowance.
A common approximation for training compute: about 6 FLOPs for every parameter for every token read. The Chinchilla paper uses it to find the best split.
The Chinchilla paper's letters: N for a model's number of parameters, D for the number of tokens it trains on.
A formula fitted to many training runs that predicts a model's loss from its size, the tokens it reads or its compute. Loss falls smoothly as they grow, by less each time.
A relationship where one quantity changes as a fixed power of another, like A / N^0.34. Each doubling of N changes it by the same share.
Each extra step helping less than the one before: every doubling of the readers' shelves lowered the loss by less.
A number in a formula chosen so the formula matches measured results. The Chinchilla formula has five: E, A, B, α and β.
The Chinchilla paper's name for its E term: the loss even a perfect model would have, because real text is never fully predictable.
In the Chinchilla paper, a perfect model of the text, the best any model could do. Its loss is the E term.
The split of a fixed compute budget between parameters and tokens that gives the lowest loss. The bottom of the valley in the sim's curve.
This case's plain name for the compute-optimal split of a budget between parameters and tokens.
Trained on too few tokens for its size: the same compute would have given a lower loss to a smaller model that read more.
Tokens read divided by parameters. Chinchilla was trained at about 20, the New Wing reader at 5 and Ottoline's at 80.
An estimate that is right on average, neither too high nor too low. The Chinchilla paper treats training loss as one for test loss, since no text is read twice.
The usual loss for a language model: how surprised it is, on average, by each real next token. Lower means it predicted the text better.
A factor of ten. Seven orders of magnitude is ten million times.
Learning more from each example or token. Kaplan and colleagues found bigger models more sample-efficient.
The procedure that adjusts numbers to fit; gradient descent from case 2 is one kind. Epoch AI found the one that fitted the Chinchilla formula stopped too early.
Redoing a published study to check that its results hold.
Improving by about the same amount each time the data is multiplied by the same factor, such as every tenfold.
What it costs to run a trained model on each request. It grows with the model's size and is paid on every call, for as long as the model is in use.
One of the biggest and most capable models the big providers sell. Usually the strongest on hard tasks, and among the most expensive per call.
A model whose parameters are published, so you can download it and run it on your own machines. Case 6 called one an open-source model.
Sorting each input into one of a fixed set of categories, like a support ticket into one of five queues.
A test set of real inputs with answers agreed in advance, kept to score every version of a system. Season 5 builds them.
A public set of test questions that many models are scored on, so their scores can be compared. It measures its own questions, not your task.
The wait for an answer: the time from sending a request to getting the reply. Eskil's readers take 0.5 to 1.4 seconds.
Sending each request to one of several models by a rule, such as whether the small one is unsure. Season 6 builds it.
To pass something to a stronger model, or a person, because the first one couldn't handle it well.
Anthropic's name for starting with a faster, cheaper model, testing it on your task, and moving up only where it falls short.
Anthropic's name for starting with the strongest model for a complex task, then moving to cheaper ones once the work is understood.
An axis where each equal step multiplies by the same amount, here by ten, so 100M, 1B and 10B sit evenly apart.
DeepMind's 2021 language model: 280 billion parameters trained on 300 billion tokens.
DeepMind's 2022 language model: 70 billion parameters trained on 1.4 trillion tokens, with the same compute as Gopher, which it outperformed. Also the paper that introduced it.
A research group that studies trends in AI, such as training compute and data.
Meta's 2024 family of open-weight language models, at 8B and 70B parameters at first release.

atWork: Find one feature at work that calls a language model, and ask why it uses the model it does. A common story: a team sends every request to the largest model, even for a simple classification task like sorting tickets into five queues, and the bill and the latency grow with the traffic. Take fifty to a hundred real inputs, write down the right answers, and agree a bar before you run anything. Then run the model you use and one or two smaller ones on them. For each, note the score, the price per million tokens times your real monthly volume, the latency, and where it sends your data. If a smaller one clears the bar, you've found money and time on every call. If none does, keep the big one, and look at whether a smaller one could take the easy cases and send it only the hard ones.

recall.prompt: Your team sends every incoming support email to the largest frontier model just to sort it into one of five queues. The monthly bill keeps climbing and replies feel slow. Your manager asks whether something cheaper would do. How do you decide, and what do you put in place?

keyIdeas.idea: Build a test from real emails with the right queue known, and agree the bar before scoring
Run smaller models on it, from the smallest up, and keep the cheapest one that passes
Compare price per token at the real volume, latency, and where the data goes
Send the cases the small one is unsure of to the big one, and re-run the test after changes

recall.model: I'd decide with our own test, not the model's size. I'd take a few hundred real emails, have someone who knows the queues label the right one for each, and agree the accuracy we need before scoring anything. Then I'd run the current frontier model and two or three smaller ones on that test set, from the smallest up. For each I'd note the accuracy, the price per million tokens times our real monthly volume, the latency, and where it sends customers' emails. If a small model clears the bar, it goes in, and the emails it's unsure of get routed to the frontier model, so the big bill only applies to the hard cases. I'd keep the test and re-run it whenever the model, the prompt or the kind of email changes, and monitor the queues for misroutes after launch.

recall.prompt: Ottoline's reader and the New Wing's used the same compute, 4.8 × 10^20 FLOPs. Why did the smaller one end up with the lower loss?
options: Smaller models always beat bigger ones once both finish training on the same books
It was trained at a lower temperature, so it settled on safer, more careful answers
It read four times the tokens, which cut loss more than four times the parameters
Its compute was counted differently, so it really had about four times as much
recall.why: At 4.8 × 10^20 FLOPs the formula's best split is about 1.31B parameters on 61.1 billion tokens. Ottoline's 1B on 80 billion sits near it at 2.408; the New Wing's 4B on 20 billion is well past it at 2.447. Smaller doesn't always win: at a fixed budget there is a best split, and too big misses it as surely as too small. Temperature is a decoding setting from case 6, not part of training.

recall.prompt: A new teammate asks what scaling laws are and what the Chinchilla paper changed. Explain it in plain words.

keyIdeas.idea: Loss falls smoothly and predictably as parameters, data and compute grow, so small runs can predict big ones
Each step up helps less: diminishing returns, with a floor set by the data
For a fixed compute budget, grow parameters and tokens together, roughly doubling tokens with each doubling of size
Many big models were undertrained: 70B on 1.4 trillion tokens beat 280B on 300 billion with the same compute

recall.model: A scaling law is a formula fitted to many training runs: a model's loss falls smoothly and predictably as you add parameters, training data and compute, so you can predict a big run from small ones. Each step helps less than the last, and if you keep the data fixed, the data sets a floor that more parameters can't get under. Earlier work read the curves as saying extra compute should go mostly into bigger models. Chinchilla, from DeepMind in 2022, found that for a fixed compute budget you should grow parameters and tokens together, roughly doubling the tokens each time you double the size, and that many big models of the day were undertrained. It proved the point with a 70B model trained on 1.4 trillion tokens, which beat the 280B Gopher, trained on 300 billion tokens with the same compute.

recall.prompt: Which is the strongest reason to put a small model into production?
options: It scores highest on the most famous public benchmark this month
It clears the bar on your own test set, at lower cost and latency
Small models never hallucinate, because there is less to go wrong
Its makers say it is nearly as good as their largest frontier model
recall.why: A model is chosen by your own task. Eskil's reading room reader clears 340 with 352, for $60 a month and 0.5 seconds an answer. A public benchmark measures its own questions, any model can hallucinate, as case 6 showed, and a maker's claim isn't a measurement.

recall.prompt: Next year's allowance is 9.6 × 10^20 FLOPs. Ignoring how many books the library owns, which split does the formula predict the lowest loss for?
recall.why: All four cost 6 × N × D = 9.6 × 10^20 FLOPs. The formula gives 2.479, 2.401, 2.333 and 2.385. The best split is about 1.79B on 89.3 billion tokens, also 2.333, and 2B on 80 billion sits almost on it. Too big starves a model of reading; too small leaves it unable to hold what it reads.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. The reading room reader has been on every desk since the vote, with about one question in ten sent up to the hosted model, names stripped. Last week a vendor offered Mr Crabbe a new 3B model that tops a famous public benchmark, at a quarter of the hosted model's price, and he wants it on every desk on Monday in place of both. Since the city archive shut in July, half the website's questions are about old street plans. The enquiry book has eleven of those.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What would you check before Monday, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: A public score isn't your task: run the new model on the library's own questions against the bar, beside the current reader
The traffic has moved: add real street-plan questions with known answers before trusting any score
Weigh latency, volume and where patrons' words go, then keep the smallest that passes
Don't switch every desk at once: trial it on a slice, with the current reader as the fallback and unsure questions still sent up

coldCase.model: A score on a public benchmark isn't a score on our desks. Before Monday I'd run the 3B model on our own test, the enquiry book against Mrs Quarmby's 340, side by side with the reading room reader. But the traffic has moved: half the website's questions are now about street plans and the book has only eleven of those, so I'd add a few dozen real street-plan questions with known answers checked by the reference librarians, and score every candidate again, the current pair included. If the 3B clears the bar, I'd compare it at our real volume, its latency, and where it runs, since a vendor's model may send patrons' words out of the building. And I wouldn't switch every desk at once: one desk or a slice of the website first, the reading room reader as the fallback, and the unsure questions still sent up while we watch the scores.

next: Next, It Remembers Nothing: a hotel guest who forgets everything each morning, and knows only what is written on the card beside his bed.

sources.title: Hoffmann, Borgeaud, Mensch and colleagues (DeepMind), Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models, arXiv 2203.15556, March 2022: current large language models are significantly undertrained, a consequence of the recent focus on scaling language models whilst keeping the amount of training data constant; over 400 language models from 70 million to over 16 billion parameters on 5 to 500 billion tokens; for compute-optimal training, model size and training tokens should be scaled equally, doubling tokens with every doubling of model size; Chinchilla, 70B parameters on 1.4 trillion tokens, same compute budget as Gopher, outperforms Gopher (280B, 300 billion tokens, Table 1); both trained for the same number of FLOPs; being 4 times smaller, memory footprint and inference cost are smaller; Kaplan et al. suggested 5.5 times the size and 1.8 times the tokens for 10 times the compute, with a fixed number of training tokens and learning rate schedule for all models; most large models trained for about 300 billion tokens; training loss treated as an unbiased estimate of test loss as the training tokens are fewer than the corpus holds (footnote 2); parametric form L(N, D) = E + A/N^alpha + B/D^beta (equation 2, section 3.3) with E = 1.69, A = 406.4, B = 410.7, alpha = 0.34, beta = 0.28 (equation 10, Appendix D.2); FLOPs(N, D) approximated as 6ND and the efficient frontier in closed form (equation 4); the third approach predicts even smaller models being optimal at larger compute budgets; Figure 4 projects 40B parameters for the Gopher budget; Gopher budget 5.76 × 10^23 FLOPs (Figure 2); Approaches 1 and 2 project 67B and 63B

Kaplan, McCandlish, Henighan, Brown, Chess, Child, Gray, Radford, Wu and Amodei (OpenAI), Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models, arXiv 2001.08361, January 2020: empirical scaling laws for language model performance on the cross-entropy loss; the loss scales as a power-law with model size, dataset size, and the amount of compute used for training, with some trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude; network width or depth have minimal effects within a wide range; larger models are significantly more sample-efficient, such that optimally compute-efficient training involves training very large models on a relatively modest amount of data and stopping significantly before convergence

Besiroglu, Erdil, Barnett and You (Epoch AI), Chinchilla Scaling: A replication attempt, arXiv 2404.10102, April 2024, revised May 2024: the reported Approach 3 estimates are inconsistent with the first two methods and fail to fit the reconstructed data; the optimizer used by Hoffmann et al. stopped before convergence, and the parameter estimates reported in the body of the paper are rounded in a way that results in substantial bias; Hoffmann et al.'s estimates suggest about 70 tokens per parameter against the 20 used to train Chinchilla; refit E = 1.8172, A = 482.01, B = 2085.43, alpha = 0.3478, beta = 0.3658 (equation 3), implying about 20 tokens per parameter, compatible with the first two methods

Meta, Introducing Meta Llama 3: The most capable openly available LLM to date, April 18, 2024: scaling laws allow us to predict the performance of our largest models on key tasks before we actually train the models; the Chinchilla-optimal amount of training compute for an 8B parameter model corresponds to ~200B tokens, yet performance continues to improve after two orders of magnitude more data; 8B and 70B models continued to improve log-linearly after training on up to 15T tokens; smaller models are generally preferred because they are much more efficient during inference

Anthropic, Choosing the right model (Claude Platform docs), as checked in October 2026: choosing a model means balancing capabilities, speed, and cost; efficiency-first: begin with a faster, more cost-effective model, test your use case thoroughly, evaluate if performance meets your requirements, upgrade only if necessary for specific capability gaps, best for tight latency requirements, cost-sensitive implementations and high-volume, straightforward tasks; capability-first: implement with the strongest starting point, then optimize to more efficient models; create benchmark tests specific to your use case, having a good evaluation set is the most important step; test with your actual prompts and data; multi-model strategies pair a lower-cost model with a frontier model so that most tokens are billed at the lower rate, including an executor that escalates hard decisions to an advisor
